The adjacency list's two costs are asymmetric with the matrix's two costs, not simply 'the list is cheap and the matrix is expensive': the list is cheap to enumerate (O(degree)) but slow to test one edge (O(min degree)); the matrix inverts this exactly (O(1) edge test, O(V) enumeration).

items.item: The list only wins on space when the graph is genuinely sparse; Wikipedia's own crossover analysis puts the break-even around a density of 1/64 for a naive array-based list against a bit-packed matrix, so 'the list is always smaller' is not stated as universal.

A weighted multigraph's parallel edges cannot both keep their own distinct weight in one matrix cell at all — a stronger, more precise claim than 'the matrix can't handle multigraphs', which is false for an unweighted multigraph (a count works fine there).

items.item: 'Which representation each later algorithm assumes' is a real trade-off against this topic's own stated costs, not folklore ('BFS uses adjacency lists, full stop'): an algorithm that repeatedly tests specific-pair membership genuinely wants the matrix instead.

An algorithm that keeps asking whether one specific pair is connected wants the matrix's O(1) lookup instead. The edge list is what you start with, before any of the other two exists.

items.item: A loop (a self-edge) is a case the sources treat specially (forbidden in a simple graph; the matrix's diagonal convention differs by directed/undirected once loops are allowed) — this topic's own graph is loop-free, and that choice is stated rather than silently assumed.

An edge list's space is exactly Θ(E), with no O(V) term at all — strictly smaller than the adjacency list's own V + E once a graph has isolated (zero-degree) vertices, which the adjacency list still pays a per-vertex cost for even though they contribute no edges.

items.item: The adjacency list's own edge-existence cost is O(min(deg(u), deg(v))), proportional to the smaller of the two vertices' own degrees, not loosely 'O(degree)' without naming which vertex's degree is searched.

items.item: This topic's own handoff does not claim the adjacency list is simply bad at scale; a graph whose edges mutate (insertions, deletions) still wants a list (or a hash-set-backed variant), since compressed sparse row's own two-pass construction assumes a largely static edge set — the trade is scale-and-staticity, not a strict improvement.
